Subagents read the coordinator's context from a shared scratchpad maintained by the SDK

SG-D1-02.rationale: Subagents run in isolated contexts and do NOT inherit the coordinator's history. Everything they need must be injected into their prompt, ideally as structured data that preserves content + metadata (citation_id, source, date, confidence).

SG-D1-03.stem: Follow-up summary queries to a multi-agent system take 40+ seconds. Investigation shows the coordinator spawns a synthesis subagent every time, passing 80k tokens of findings it already holds. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Compress the findings before passing to the subagent
Increase the synthesis subagent's context window
Have the coordinator answer the follow-up directly using its existing context
Cache the synthesis subagent's responses
Use fork_session to speed up spawning

SG-D1-03.rationale: Spawning a subagent to reprocess data the coordinator already holds is an anti-pattern. Subagents are for new exploration, not redundant re-synthesis. fork_session is for divergent exploration branches, not for fixing latency.

SG-D1-04.stem: A document analysis subagent processes 12 legal precedents sequentially, taking 3+ minutes. How do you reduce latency?

options.text: Increase the subagent's context window
Have the coordinator emit multiple Task tool calls in a single response so subagents run in parallel
Use fork_session to speed up processing
Use the Message Batches API

SG-D1-04.rationale: Emitting several Task tool_use blocks in the same turn launches subagents in parallel: total latency goes from the SUM of all tasks to the MAXIMUM of a single one. The Batch API has a 24-hour SLA and is not suited to latency-sensitive work.

SG-D1-06.stem: Every pull request must be reviewed for code style, security, and documentation. Which decomposition pattern fits best?

options.text: Dynamic subagent decomposition — the coordinator decides which checks to run per PR
A routing agent that picks one specialist (style, security, OR docs) per PR
A single massive prompt asking one agent to evaluate all three aspects together
Prompt chaining: sequential isolated passes for style, security, docs, then merge

SG-D1-06.rationale: Prompt chaining is the right pattern when the flow is predictable, mandatory, and always the same. Isolating distinct cognitive lenses prevents attention dilution. Dynamic decomposition is for open-ended, unpredictable research.

SG-D1-07.stem: A multi-agent research pipeline crashed after processing 12 of 18 documents. How do you resume?

options.text: Run --resume on the crashed session
Use fork_session from the crash point
Write completed findings to a structured checkpoint file, start a fresh session, and inject the checkpoint as structured context
Resume the session and let the agent re-discover state organically

SG-D1-07.rationale: Tool results from a crashed session are stale and unreliable. Extract the durable state to a JSON checkpoint, start from scratch, and inject the explicit state (done / partial / pending) per item. fork_session is for divergent branches, not for recovery.

SG-D1-08.stem: After an agent reviews a 12-file codebase, a developer edits 3 of the files. What is the most efficient way to update the review?

options.text: Resume the session, explicitly tell the agent which 3 files changed, and ask it to re-analyze only those in the context of prior findings
Start a fresh session and re-analyze all 12 files
Resume silently and trust the agent to notice the diffs
Create a new session with only the 3 modified files

SG-D1-08.rationale: When most of the context is still valid, resume and report the delta in a structured way. Discarding the other 9 files breaks cross-file context. Resuming silently produces stale reasoning because the agent may not re-read the changed files.

SG-D1-09.stem: A web-search subagent is given exact queries, source priorities, and date filters. It reports 'insufficient results' instead of trying alternatives. What fixes the rigidity best?

options.text: Add a fallback: 'report failure if fewer than 5 results'
Replace step-by-step procedural instructions with a goal + quality-criteria prompt
Expand the exact query list to cover more emerging topics
Use generic single-word queries to broaden the search

SG-D1-09.rationale: Over-specifying turns the subagent into a rigid executor that gives up at dead ends. Declaring intent, minimum quality thresholds, and source criteria lets it form its own queries.

SG-D1-10.stem: Search and analysis subagents have finished. The coordinator spawns a synthesis subagent. How should it provide the findings?

options.text: Let the synthesis subagent re-run the search and analysis tools
Let the synthesis subagent read from the coordinator's session history
Pass a prose summary of the findings
Pass complete findings in the prompt using a structured format that separates content from metadata (claim, evidence, source, date)

SG-D1-10.rationale: The structured handoff preserves provenance. Prose summaries collapse metadata and lose attribution. Inheriting session history is architecturally impossible. Re-running tools violates scope and wastes cost and latency.

SG-D2-03.stem: Users refer to databases by ambiguous names ('research database' instead of 'db_res_01'). How should the tool schema handle this?

options.text: Use an enum parameter listing the allowed backend names
Use a freeform string with backend fuzzy matching
Allow freeform but reject at runtime if incorrect
Default to searching all databases simultaneously

SG-D2-03.rationale: Enums put the constraint in the schema, so the model uses its semantic understanding to map the ambiguous input to the exact backend values BEFORE execution. Fuzzy matching pushes the ambiguity to the infrastructure; runtime rejection wastes a turn; searching all databases drives up cost, latency, and context bloat.

SG-D2-05.stem: Your tool experiences both network timeouts and user-syntax errors. How should each be handled?

options.text: Auto-retry both 3 times before returning failure
Pass all errors to the agent for retry
Auto-retry transient errors internally; return syntax/validation errors immediately with explicit details so the agent can self-correct
Return generic 'failed' messages for both

SG-D2-05.rationale: Transient failures are system-level: they are handled with retry logic in the backend, not by burning LLM turns. Validation errors need the model's reasoning: return them with detail (which field, why it is invalid). Retrying a malformed UUID three times is pure waste.

SG-D2-07.stem: An extract_metadata tool returns a DOI. lookup_citations and verify_doi need the DOI. The model sometimes calls the enrichment tools first and they fail. How do you enforce order?

options.text: Add a prompt instruction: 'always call extract_metadata first'
Set tool_choice to force extract_metadata on turn 1, then switch to 'auto' on subsequent turns
Merge all three tools into one
Use 'auto' and shorten the enrichment-tool descriptions

SG-D2-07.rationale: tool_choice = {type: 'tool', name: 'extract_metadata'} is a deterministic gate at the API level. Prompt instructions are probabilistic. Merging tools destroys composability.

SG-D2-08.stem: A third-party MCP server's tools are annotated readOnlyHint=true. Can you safely bypass user confirmation for those tools?

options.text: Yes, because readOnlyHint guarantees no side effects
Yes, because the MCP server runs locally
No — MCP annotations are self-reported, untrusted metadata. Base confirmation bypass on explicit trust in the vendor/server itself, not on the labels
Only after sandbox testing confirms read-only behavior

SG-D2-08.rationale: readOnlyHint and destructiveHint are HINTS declared by the MCP server. A malicious or buggy server can lie. Trust must be anchored in vendor verification, not in the annotations.

SG-D2-10.stem: update_game_score(date, team_name) keeps failing due to ambiguous nicknames, same-day rematches, and date format variations. Best fix?

options.text: Require strict ISO-8601 dates and official team names in the schema
Add formatting examples in the tool description
Add regex validation
Introduce search_games that returns a game_id, and make update_score require game_id only

SG-D2-10.rationale: Natural-language attributes are inherently ambiguous as database keys. Separate discovery (search_games → game_id) from action (update_score(game_id, ...)). Strict formatting does not resolve rematches; regex does not disambiguate.

SG-D2-11.stem: Agents repeatedly chain get_property_details(property_id) -> get_neighborhood_info(address). How should you fix the chaining cost?

options.text: Merge into one get_all_property_data tool
Make get_neighborhood_info accept property_id and resolve the address internally
Improve prompts to extract the address more reliably
Add a middle-tier helper tool

SG-D2-11.rationale: If a tool always logically depends on a mechanical ID→string lookup, internalize that lookup. Forcing the agent to orchestrate purely mechanical chains wastes tokens and latency and creates failure surface. But do not over-merge conceptually distinct tools.

SG-D2-12.stem: What is the primary advantage of enforcing structured JSON output for tool responses?

options.text: It makes the LLM's reasoning deterministic
It guarantees the data is semantically correct
It reduces token consumption vs. plain text
It lets downstream systems access specific fields directly without parsing free-form text

SG-D2-12.rationale: Structured output enforces FORM, not truth: JSON does not validate semantics. It also typically INCREASES tokens (braces, keys). The gain is reliable field access for chained tools.

SG-D2-13.stem: A search tool returns all matching records, causing latency and context bloat. Best redesign?

options.text: Silently limit to top 5 most relevant
Return the first page + pagination metadata (total_count, next_cursor) so the agent can fetch more if needed
Create a separate fetch_next_page tool
Add a max_pages parameter and let the agent fetch internally

SG-D2-13.rationale: First page + cursor + total gives the agent situational awareness to decide whether it already has enough. Silent truncation hides information. A separate fetch_next_page tool bloats the toolset. Internal multi-page fetching hides latency and tokens.

SG-D2-14.stem: Multiple shipping-carrier APIs return timestamps, statuses, and delay codes in different JSON shapes. How should the agent see them?

options.text: Pass raw JSON and instruct the agent how to parse each carrier
Normalize all carrier responses into one common schema (status, estimated_delivery, etc.) before returning to the agent
Create a separate tracking tool per carrier
Return both normalized + raw for max context

SG-D2-14.rationale: Agents reason better over consistent shapes. Heterogeneous schemas force attention toward parsing instead of the task. PostToolUse hooks are a natural place to normalize. Including the raw response is noise that consumes context.

SG-D2-15.stem: Agents frequently call delete_file when archive_file is correct. Most direct fix?

options.text: Expand both tool descriptions to define purpose, boundaries, and explicit 'when NOT to use' guidance
Add a confirmation prompt inside delete_file
Remove delete_file entirely
Add few-shot examples in the system prompt

SG-D2-15.rationale: Descriptions are the highest-leverage selection signal. Include negative constraints ('Do not use for backup files — use archive_file'). Few-shot helps, but descriptions are the structural fix. Confirmation prompts protect against harm but do not correct the upstream wrong choice.

SG-D3-06.stem: You're about to refactor a service touching 30 files across 4 modules with three plausible designs. Plan Mode or direct execution?

options.text: Direct — just start editing and iterate
Plan Mode — large multi-file changes with multiple plausible approaches benefit from explicit planning before writes
Either — they're equivalent
Plan Mode is only for new projects

SG-D3-06.rationale: Plan mode is for architectural decisions, multi-file changes, and choosing between several approaches. Direct execution is for single-file edits, clear-cut fixes, and simple additions. Plan mode produces a reviewed plan that you approve before any writes begin.

SG-D4-05.stem: Invoice extraction sometimes produces line items that don't sum to the stated total. Best architectural fix?

options.text: Add a calculated_total field, compare to stated_total, flag mismatches for human review
Automatically adjust line items to match the stated total
Run a secondary LLM step to reconcile the math
Add more few-shot examples of correct math

SG-D4-05.rationale: JSON schemas protect syntax, not semantics. Extract both the declared value and the calculated value, and flag discrepancies deterministically. Auto-correcting fabricates data; a second LLM pass adds non-deterministic overhead; few-shot examples cannot enforce arithmetic.

SG-D4-08.stem: You must process documents within 30 hours via the Batch API (which takes up to 24h). What submission cadence minimizes risk while keeping the cost discount?

options.text: Submit every 6 hours
Submit one big batch at end of day
Use synchronous API instead
Submit every 4 hours

SG-D4-08.rationale: Worst-case wait = batch interval + 24h of processing. Every 4h: 4 + 24 = 28h (2h of margin). Every 6h: 6 + 24 = 30h (zero margin = SLA risk). End of day: 24 + 24 = 48h (violates the SLA). Synchronous processing wastes the 50% discount.

SG-D4-09.stem: A 10,000-doc batch finishes; 300 documents fail with context_length_exceeded. Most cost-effective recovery?

options.text: Resubmit all 10,000 with smaller chunks
Switch the 300 to the synchronous API
Use the custom_id to extract only the 300 failed docs, chunk them, and resubmit as a new batch
Increase the model's context window setting

SG-D4-09.rationale: Resubmitting the 9,700 successful ones is pure waste. Chunking applies only to the documents that actually exceed the limit. Synchronous processing costs twice as much with no latency benefit when chunking is still required anyway. Context limits are constants of the model.

SG-D4-10.stem: Test on 500 docs shows 18% require 2-3 prompt refinements. You need to process 50,000 docs via Batch API. Strategy?

options.text: Refine the prompt on a representative sample first, then batch all 50,000
Batch all 50,000 immediately and resubmit failures
Use synchronous API on all 50,000 to refine per-doc
Submit 5,000-doc batches incrementally to learn failure modes

SG-D4-10.rationale: Iterative refinement at scale destroys the Batch API's cost advantage. Resubmission cycles are expensive; synchronous processing throws away the 50% discount; incremental learning still keeps paying for failure cycles at scale.

SG-D4-12.stem: A technical manual lists two different battery capacities (in prose and in a specs table). The specs table is right 90% of the time. Schema design?

options.text: Halt and require manual correction
Single-value schema; let the model pick the most likely value
Hard-code: always extract from the specs table
Schema captures all conflicting values + source locations to preserve provenance

SG-D4-12.rationale: Collapsing prematurely to a single value destroys the evidence. Hardcoding the specification table fails 10% of the time. Preserve the conflict structurally and let business logic or human review resolve it.

SG-D5-02.stem: On a 200k-token model, documents under 150k tokens give 98% accuracy. On documents 175k-185k tokens, accuracy drops to 71% and content in the final third is consistently missing. Most likely cause?

options.text: Tool definitions + system prompt consume input tokens, pushing the total payload near the absolute context limit and degrading attention near the end
Schemas with 8-10 fields inherently raise decision complexity
The model's effective attention span is shorter than its window
The model spreads attention proportionally, leaving the end starved

SG-D5-02.rationale: Context is an absolute budget. A 2,500-token schema plus a 1,500-token system prompt leaves ~196k for the document. Near the limit, attention degrades, and the symptom matches 'the final third is missing' (a boundary effect, not a lost-in-the-middle effect). Fix: trim the schema, chunk the document, or use a model with a larger context window.

SG-D5-04.stem: Web search agent gathered 120k raw tokens, doc analysis extracted 15k tokens of insights, synthesis produced a 3k-token narrative draft. What should you pass to the report-generation agent?

options.text: All 120k raw tokens + intermediate outputs
Only the 3k synthesis narrative
Synthesis narrative + full doc-analysis reasoning chain
Synthesis narrative + a lean structured citation index (with claim, source, key_quote) + any conflict flags

SG-D5-04.rationale: Raw content triggers lost-in-the-middle. Narrative alone causes hallucinated citations. Reasoning chains are internal noise. The optimal handoff is dense narrative plus compact, structured citation metadata.

SG-D5-06.stem: Extraction is 97% accurate overall at confidence >= 90%. You plan to auto-process high-confidence extractions. Most critical pre-deployment check?

options.text: Segment accuracy by document type AND field
Deploy globally at the >=90% threshold
Run a random sample review across all docs
Raise the threshold to >=95% to be safe

SG-D5-06.rationale: An aggregate 97% can hide catastrophic per-segment rates (standard invoices at 99% but handwritten forms at 61%). Random sampling under-represents rare, difficult cases. Raising the threshold without stratifying still sends unknown per-segment error rates into production.

SG-EP01.stem: An automated invoice extraction pipeline occasionally outputs structured JSON where the extracted line items do not add up to the total amount extracted from the invoice. What is the best architectural approach to handle this semantic error?

options.text: Add a calculated_total field alongside the stated_total field, compare them, and flag mismatches for human review.
Automatically adjust the line item values so they mathematically sum to the stated total.
Introduce a secondary LLM step to reconcile the math errors.
Add more few-shot examples of correct math to the prompt.

SG-EP01.rationale: JSON schemas prevent syntax errors, not semantic ones. The most robust self-correction pattern is to extract what the document declares and what the model calculates; if they don't match, the record is flagged for human review. B fabricates values not backed by the document; C adds unnecessary architectural overhead; D cannot guarantee deterministic arithmetic consistency.

SG-EP02.stem: You are preparing to process 50,000 legacy documents using the Batch API. An initial test on 500 documents reveals that 18% of them require 2-3 prompt refinements to extract data correctly. What is the most cost-efficient strategy for scaling this workload?

options.text: Refine the prompt interactively on a representative sample to maximize first-pass success, then process all 50,000 documents via the Batch API.
Use the Batch API to process all 50,000 documents immediately, identify failures at scale, and resubmit them.
Process the 50,000 documents using the synchronous API to handle prompt refinement dynamically per document.
Begin submitting 5,000-document batches to incrementally learn failure modes in production.

SG-EP02.rationale: Refine the prompt on a representative sample BEFORE processing large volumes. Iterative resubmissions at scale destroy the Batch API's savings.

SG-EP03.stem: Your system processes asynchronous user requests with a strict SLA requiring results within 30 hours of submission. You plan to use the Message Batches API, which can take up to 24 hours to complete. Which batch submission schedule best meets the SLA while maximizing cost efficiency?

options.text: Submit batches every 6 hours.
Submit one large batch at the end of each day.
Use the synchronous API instead to guarantee the SLA.
Submit batches every 4 hours.

SG-EP03.rationale: The worst-case time is the wait until the next window plus 24h of processing. Every 4h gives 28h with 2h of margin; every 6h gives exactly 30h with no margin; end of day gives 48h and violates the SLA.

SG-EP04.stem: An extraction pipeline processes technical manuals. A specific manual lists two conflicting battery capacities: one in the text and a different one in a detailed specs table. Historical data shows the specs table is correct 90% of the time. How should the extraction schema handle this?

options.text: Halt processing and flag the document for manual correction before extraction.
Use a single-value schema and prompt the model to pick the most likely correct value.
Hard-code a rule to always extract the value from the specs table.
Change the field to capture all conflicting values along with their source locations to preserve provenance for downstream reconciliation.

SG-EP04.rationale: Forcing a premature collapse to a single value is an anti-pattern. If the table is right 90% of the time, hardcoding a preference guarantees a 10% error rate. An array of values with source location preserves full provenance.

SG-EP05.stem: An agent uses a search_documents tool to find files, and subsequently uses share_document(document_id, email) and move_document(document_id, folder) to act on them. How should search_documents format its output to ensure reliable chaining?

options.text: Return clickable human-readable URLs.
Return structured data containing document_id and metadata for each result.
Return detailed prose summaries of the document contents.
Return a simple list of document titles.

SG-EP05.rationale: Multi-step flows require clear input/output contracts. Since downstream tools require document_id, the search tool must return exactly that identifier in structured format alongside the human-readable metadata.

SG-EP06.stem: When designing agentic workflows, what is the primary advantage of enforcing structured JSON output for tool responses and agent outputs?

options.text: It makes the LLM's reasoning process perfectly deterministic.
It ensures the semantic truth of the data fetched from backend APIs.
It significantly reduces token consumption compared to standard text.
It allows the agent and downstream systems to reliably access specific fields directly without parsing free-form text.

SG-EP06.rationale: Structured output provides a stable schema contract. JSON enforces form, not truth, and tends to increase token consumption due to repeated braces.

SG-EP07.stem: An agent has access to over 50 different API connector tools. During execution, it frequently selects the wrong connector, even when explicitly instructed to search first. What is the most effective architectural change to fix this tool selection failure?

options.text: Rewrite the tool descriptions for all 50 connectors to be more detailed.
Combine all 50 connectors into a single monolithic API call.
Implement better error handling so the agent can recover after selecting the wrong connector.
Provide a search_connectors tool that dynamically scopes the available tool set, exposing only the relevant matched connectors to the agent.

SG-EP07.rationale: Exposing 50+ tools degrades decision accuracy. The fix is dynamic scoping: the agent first calls search_connectors, and the system injects only the 2-3 relevant tools in the next turn. Better descriptions help but don't solve the systemic cognitive overload.

SG-EP08.stem: An agent needs to query specific internal databases, but users often refer to them using ambiguous natural language (e.g., "research database" instead of "db_res_01"). How should the tool's input schema be designed to handle this reliably?

options.text: Use an enum parameter explicitly listing the allowed database system names.
Use a freeform string parameter and use backend fuzzy matching to find the right database.
Allow freeform strings but reject the tool call at runtime if the name is incorrect.
Default to searching all databases simultaneously if the user is ambiguous.

SG-EP08.rationale: Enums create a strict input contract and let the model map messy natural language to the exact backend value before executing.

SG-EP09.stem: A search tool automatically fetches and returns all matching records from a database. This frequently causes severe latency and context bloat, as most agent tasks only need the first few results. What is the best way to redesign this tool's output?

options.text: Silently limit the results to the top 5 most relevant hits.
Return the first page of results along with pagination metadata (e.g., total count, cursor) so the agent can fetch more if needed.
Create a separate fetch_next_page tool for the agent to use.
Add a max_pages parameter to let the agent decide how many pages to fetch internally.

SG-EP09.rationale: Returning the first page with total_matches and next_cursor gives the agent situational awareness to decide whether it needs more.

SG-EP10.stem: A third-party MCP server provides tools annotated with readOnlyHint=true. You are designing the user confirmation flow for your agent application. How should you treat these tool annotations?

options.text: Trust the annotations automatically because the MCP server runs locally.
Treat the annotations as untrusted metadata, and base your confirmation bypass policy on your trust of the vendor/server, not the self-reported labels.
Infer the server's trustworthiness by testing the tools in a sandbox first.
Bypass user confirmations safely, as the readOnlyHint guarantees no destructive actions can occur.

SG-EP10.rationale: Annotations are self-reported by the MCP server. If the server is third-party and unverified, its metadata is not a security boundary.

SG-EP11.stem: An agent frequently executes a two-step sequence: it calls get_property_details(property_id) to find an address, then passes that address to get_neighborhood_info(address). This chaining increases latency and failure rates. How should the tool design be improved?

options.text: Merge both tools into a single get_all_property_data tool.
Modify get_neighborhood_info to accept property_id directly and resolve the address internally.
Improve the prompt to ensure the agent extracts the address more reliably.
Create a middle-tier helper tool to manage the data handoff.

SG-EP11.rationale: Forcing the agent to orchestrate a purely mechanical ID-to-string lookup wastes tokens, adds a point of failure, and increases latency. Merging everything over-consolidates distinct capabilities.

SG-EP12.stem: An agent tracks shipments using tools that call multiple different shipping carrier APIs. Each carrier returns timestamps, statuses, and delay codes in completely different JSON formats. How should you design the tool output provided to the agent?

options.text: Pass the raw JSON to the agent and provide extensive prompt instructions on how to parse each carrier's format.
Normalize the carrier responses into a single common schema (e.g., status, estimated_delivery) before returning it to the agent.
Create separate tracking tools for each carrier to keep the raw schemas distinct.
Return both the normalized schema and the full raw response to maximize context.

SG-EP12.rationale: Agents reason better over consistent structures. Dumping heterogeneous schemas forces the LLM to spend attention parsing formats instead of solving the problem.

SG-EP13.stem: An agent updates sports scores using an update_game_score(date, team_name) tool. The tool frequently fails due to ambiguous team nicknames, rematches on the same day, and date format variations. What is the most reliable tool design to fix this?

options.text: Require strict ISO-8601 date formats and official full team names in the tool schema.
Improve the tool description to provide examples of correct formatting.
Add regex validation to the tool parameters to catch formatting errors early.
Introduce a search_games tool that returns a game_id, and update the scoring tool to accept only the game_id.

SG-EP13.rationale: Natural-language attributes are fragile as keys. Separate discovery from action with a machine identifier.

SG-EP14.stem: An agent processes employee reimbursements. Company policy dictates that payouts over $500 must go to a pending approval queue and cannot be disbursed automatically. You need to ensure this threshold absolutely cannot be bypassed by the agent. Where should this rule be enforced?

options.text: Add a requires_approval boolean parameter to the tool schema that the agent must set.
Enforce the $500 threshold inside the process_reimbursement tool logic itself.
Write a strict system prompt instructing the agent to never disburse amounts over $500.
Provide two separate tools (disburse and request_approval) and trust the agent to select correctly.

SG-EP14.rationale: If a rule can NOT be skipped, it must be enforced deterministically in the backend. Implementing the threshold inside the tool's code guarantees that even with hallucination or prompt injection, the payment degrades to 'pending approval'.

SG-EP15.stem: During execution, an agent repeatedly struggles to format inputs correctly for user_id and fields_to_update when calling an update tool. What is the most effective way to help the model understand exactly what values and formats to provide?

options.text: Write clear, detailed parameter descriptions in the tool schema.
Make the JSON schema extremely strict with complex regex constraints.
Rename the tool to include formatting hints in the tool name itself.
Add error-handling logic that explains the formatting rules only when the tool fails.

SG-EP15.rationale: Tool and parameter descriptions are the primary mechanism by which the model understands the expected inputs. Strict validation rejects bad inputs but doesn't teach it to generate good ones; reactive error messages waste turns.

SG-EP16.stem: A tool experiences two types of errors: transient network timeouts, and permanent user syntax errors. How should the tool handle these errors to optimize the agent workflow?

options.text: Pass all errors to the agent and prompt it to retry timeouts but stop on syntax errors.
Automatically retry transient network timeouts inside the tool, but immediately return syntax errors with clear validation details to the agent.
Uniformly auto-retry all errors 3 times before returning a failure message to the agent.
Return all errors immediately to the agent as generic 'Tool Execution Failed' messages.

SG-EP16.rationale: Agents shouldn't spend tokens and turns resolving predictable transient errors; those belong in backend retry loops. Syntax errors do require the agent's reasoning and should be returned immediately with explicit details.

SG-EP17.stem: An agent has access to an archive_file tool and a delete_file tool. It frequently calls delete_file when it should have archived a backup file. What is the most direct way to fix this tool selection error?

options.text: Expand the tool descriptions to clearly define the purpose, boundaries, and specific scenarios where archiving is preferred over deleting.
Add a confirmation prompt directly inside the delete_file tool logic.
Remove the delete_file tool entirely and handle deletions via a separate batch process.
Provide few-shot examples in the system prompt showing correct usage.

SG-EP17.rationale: Tool descriptions are the highest-leverage mechanism for fixing selection errors. When two tools overlap, their descriptions must define explicit negative constraints. The confirmation prompt guards against harm but does not fix the choice.

SG-EP18.stem: You are using an agent to analyze a 12-file codebase. After the agent completes its initial review, a developer modifies 3 of the files. You want the agent to update its findings efficiently. What is the best approach?

options.text: Resume the session, explicitly inform the agent which 3 files changed, and instruct it to re-analyze only those files in the context of its prior findings.
Start a completely fresh session and have the agent re-analyze all 12 files from scratch.
Resume the session but don't explicitly mention the changes, trusting the agent to notice the file diffs organically.
Create a new session containing only the 3 modified files, discarding the context of the other 9 files.

SG-EP18.rationale: If most of the context is still valid, resuming is efficient, but the delta must be reported in a structured way. Discarding the other 9 files removes the cross-file context needed for code analysis.

SG-EP19.stem: An agent interacting with multiple MCP servers wastes significant context and time performing sequential lookup calls just to discover what data (issue tickets, docs, schemas) is available. How can you improve data discovery?

options.text: Consolidate all the MCP servers into a single, massive endpoint.
Add a new discover_data tool to every MCP server.
Implement keyword-based routing in the coordinator to send queries to the right server automatically.
Expose each MCP server's content catalog as an MCP Resource, allowing the agent to read what data exists before making targeted tool calls.

SG-EP19.rationale: MCP distinguishes Tools (specific actions or queries) from Resources (available context/data). Exposing hierarchies, ticket summaries, or schemas as Resources lets the agent see what exists before deciding which calls to make, eliminating exploratory spam.

SG-EP20.stem: An agent is responsible for reviewing pull requests. Every PR must be reviewed for three specific aspects: code style, security vulnerabilities, and documentation accuracy. Which architectural pattern is best suited for this workflow?

options.text: Dynamic subagent decomposition, letting a coordinator agent decide which aspects to check case-by-case.
A routing agent that categorizes the PR and sends it to either a style, security, or docs specialist.
A single, massive prompt instructing one agent to analyze all three aspects simultaneously.
Prompt chaining: reviewing style, security, and documentation in separate sequential passes, then merging the outputs into a final synthesis.

SG-EP20.rationale: When the workflow is predictable, mandatory, and always follows the same decomposition, prompt chaining is superior. Routing would mean that only ONE of the specialists does the work, but the prompt states that ALL PRs receive all three checks.

SG-EP21.stem: In production, follow-up summarization queries to a multi-agent system take over 40 seconds. Investigation shows the coordinator agent spawns a synthesis subagent for each follow-up request, passing 80000 tokens of accumulated findings. The coordinator already holds these findings in its context. What is the most effective way to improve response time?

options.text: Compress findings before passing them to the synthesis subagent.
Increase the synthesis subagent's context window.
Handle the summarization directly using the coordinator's existing context.
Cache synthesis subagent responses.
Use fork_session to speed up subagent spawning.

SG-EP21.rationale: If the coordinator already has the findings in context, it should handle follow-up queries itself. fork_session is meant for divergent exploration branches, not for optimizing latency.

SG-EP22.stem: After web search and document analysis subagents finish their tasks, the coordinator needs to spawn a synthesis subagent to combine the findings. What is the correct approach for providing the synthesis subagent with the information it needs?

options.text: Let the synthesis subagent call the search and analysis tools itself.
Let the synthesis subagent read directly from the coordinator's session history.
Pass a prose summary of the findings to the synthesis subagent.
Pass complete findings embedded directly in the synthesis subagent's prompt using a structured format separating content from metadata.

SG-EP22.rationale: Subagents start with zero prior knowledge and do not inherit the coordinator's history. A structured format {claim, evidence, source_url, date} preserves content, provenance, and temporality.

SG-EP23.stem: A coordinator provides exact search queries, source priorities, and date filters step-by-step to a web search subagent. However, the subagent often reports "insufficient results" instead of trying alternatives, drops in quality on emerging topics, and rarely surfaces unconventional sources. What is the most effective way to improve the subagent's adaptability?

options.text: Add a fallback instruction to report failure if fewer than 5 results are found.
Replace procedural instructions with goal-oriented prompts detailing research goals and quality criteria.
Expand the exact query lists to cover emerging topics.
Provide generic, single-word queries to broaden the search base.

SG-EP23.rationale: Over-specifying turns the subagent into a rigid executor. Giving it research intent, minimum quality thresholds, and credibility criteria grants it the authority to adapt its approach.

SG-EP24.stem: A document analysis subagent processes citations in complex legal cases sequentially. A landmark case citing 12 precedents currently takes over 3 minutes to process. What is the most effective way to reduce this latency?

options.text: Increase the subagent's context window.
Have the coordinator emit multiple Task tool calls simultaneously in a single response.
Use fork_session to speed up processing.
Use the Message Batches API.

SG-EP24.rationale: Emitting all 12 Task tool calls in a single turn launches 12 subagents in parallel, reducing latency from the sum of all tasks to the duration of the longest one. The Message Batches API has an SLA of up to 24 hours and would drastically worsen latency.

SG-EP25.stem: Final reports consistently mishandle uncertainty. A web search agent returns a $50B estimate (unspecified methodology), while a document analysis agent returns a $35B estimate (±$7B, 95% CI). The coordinator either picks one arbitrarily or produces a vague, hedged statement. What approach best avoids this?

options.text: Instruct the coordinator to always prefer peer-reviewed sources.
Ask the synthesis subagent to pick the most recent figure.
Have the coordinator average the two conflicting values.
Require subagents to return structured data with methodology/confidence metadata and a conflict_detected flag to preserve both values.

SG-EP25.rationale: Prose findings lose provenance. Subagents must return structured objects {claim, source_type, methodology, confidence, date}, and a programmatic conflict_detected flag forces synthesis to present both values with their context. Averaging fabricates a number that no source supports.

SG-EP26.stem: A web search agent gathers 120k tokens of raw content, a document analysis agent extracts 15k tokens of insights, and a synthesis agent produces a 3k-token narrative draft. The coordinator must now pass context to a report generation agent for final output with proper citations. Which context-passing strategy provides the best balance?

options.text: Pass the 120k tokens of raw content and all intermediate outputs.
Pass only the 3k-token synthesis narrative.
Pass the synthesis narrative and the full document analysis reasoning chain.
Pass the synthesis narrative along with a lean, structured citation index and conflict flags.

SG-EP26.rationale: Passing 138k+ tokens of raw content wastes budget and triggers lost in the middle. Passing too little causes citation hallucination. The balance is the dense narrative plus a compact citation index {citation_id, claim, source, key_quote}.

SG-EP27.stem: A synthesis agent receives findings from upstream agents and passes a consolidated prose summary to a report generation agent. During testing, the report generator makes factual claims but cannot accurately attribute them because source metadata was lost during the summarization step. What is the most effective approach?

options.text: Ask the synthesis agent to re-include the full source text in its summary.
Assign a citation_id at the earliest agent, and require the synthesis agent to produce an inline-tagged narrative alongside a preserved structured citation index.
Instruct the report agent to infer the original sources from the claim content.
Instruct the synthesis agent to "preserve sources" in its prose output.

SG-EP27.rationale: Prose summaries destroy metadata by nature. The structural solution is to separate content from metadata: citation_id assigned at discovery, narrative with inline brackets, and the full index traveling separately.

SG-EP28.stem: A multi-agent research pipeline crashes after processing 12 out of 18 documents. Each agent has partially completed work. You need to resume the pipeline without losing the fidelity of prior findings or repeating completed work. What is the best state management approach?

options.text: Run the --resume command directly on the crashed session.
Use fork_session from the crash point to branch the execution.
Write completed findings to a structured checkpoint file, start a fresh session, and inject the checkpoint as structured context.
Resume the session without noting partial document states.

SG-EP28.rationale: After a mid-execution crash, tool results become stale. Extract the completed work to a durable JSON checkpoint, start a fresh session, and inject it indicating what is complete, what is partial (by section), and what is pending.

SG-EP30.stem: An extraction system has operated with 100% human review for 3 months. Analysis shows that extractions with a model confidence of >=90% have a 97% accuracy overall. To reduce reviewer workload, you plan to automate high-confidence extractions. Before deploying, what validation step is most critical?

options.text: Segment the accuracy metrics by document type and field.
Deploy the automation globally at the >=90% confidence threshold.
Run a random sample review across all documents before deploying.
Increase the confidence threshold to >=95% just to be safe.

SG-EP30.rationale: A 97% aggregate is dangerous because it can mask catastrophic rates within minority subsets (standard invoices 99.2% versus handwritten forms 61%). Random sampling underrepresents rare or difficult types.

SG-EP31.stem: After a daily batch of 10,000 documents completes processing, 300 documents (3%) fail with context_length_exceeded errors. The result file identifies each failure by its custom_id. What is the most cost-effective approach to process these failures?

options.text: Resubmit all 10,000 documents with a smaller chunk size.
Switch the 300 failed documents to the synchronous API.
Extract only the 300 failed documents using their custom_id, chunk them, and resubmit them as a new batch.
Increase the context window limit globally.

SG-EP31.rationale: Resubmitting the successful documents wastes 97% of the cost. Use the custom_id mapping to isolate the 300 failures, chunk them, and send them in a new batch. Context limits are fixed model constraints, not configuration.

SG-EP32.stem: An extraction system uses a 12-field JSON schema and detailed tool descriptions totaling ~2,500 tokens. For documents under 150k tokens, accuracy is 98%. However, for documents between 175k-185k tokens, accuracy drops to 71%, with information from the final third of the document consistently missing. The model's context window is 200k tokens. What is the most likely cause of this degradation?

options.text: The tool definition consumes input tokens, and combined with system prompts, pushes the total input close to the context limit, degrading attention for content at the end.
Schemas exceeding 8-10 fields inherently increase decision complexity.
Very long documents exceed the model's effective attention span causing middle-document degradation.
The model distributes attention proportionally, causing the end of the document to receive insufficient focus.

SG-EP32.rationale: Context limits are absolute. With 2,500 tokens of schema and 1,500 for the system prompt, the effective space drops to ~196k. Schema complexity would cause semantic errors, not positional omission; and lost in the middle affects the middle of the document, while here the symptom is the FINAL third.

SG-EP33.stem: A pipeline uses an extract_metadata tool that returns a DOI. It also has lookup_citations and verify_doi enrichment tools that require a DOI to function. When users ask to "extract the metadata and tell me how cited it is", the model sometimes calls the enrichment tools first, which fail because they lack the DOI. What is the most effective way to ensure structured metadata extraction happens first?

options.text: Add a prompt instruction to "always call extract_metadata first."
Set tool_choice to strictly force the extract_metadata tool on the first turn, then use tool_choice: "auto" for subsequent turns.
Combine all three tools into a single massive tool.
Use tool_choice: "auto" but restrict the descriptions of the enrichment tools.

SG-EP33.rationale: When there are strict dependencies between tools, a deterministic prerequisite gate is needed. Forcing the tool name on the first turn and releasing tool_choice to "auto" on subsequent turns is the pattern.

PE-001.stem: In 12% of cases, your agent skips the call to get_customer and uses lookup_order with only the name the customer provided, which occasionally results in misidentified accounts and incorrect refunds. What change would be most effective?

options.text: Add a programmatic prerequisite that blocks lookup_order and process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID.
Improve the system prompt to state that verification with get_customer is mandatory before any order operation.
Add few-shot examples showing the agent always calling get_customer first.
Implement a routing classifier that enables only the appropriate subset of tools per request type.

PE-001.rationale: When critical business logic requires a tool sequence, programmatic enforcement provides deterministic guarantees that prompting cannot. B and C rely on the LLM's probabilistic compliance. D addresses tool availability, not ordering.

PE-002.stem: The agent frequently calls get_customer when users ask about orders, instead of lookup_order. Both tools have minimal descriptions and accept similar identifier formats. What is the most effective first step?

options.text: Add 5 to 8 few-shot examples to the system prompt demonstrating the correct selection.
Expand each tool's description with input formats, example queries, edge cases, and boundaries explaining when to use it versus similar tools.
Implement a routing layer that parses the input and preselects the tool based on keywords.
Consolidate both into a single lookup_entity that accepts any identifier and internally decides the backend.

PE-002.rationale: Descriptions are the primary tool-selection mechanism. Few-shot examples add token overhead without fixing the root cause. The routing layer is overengineered, and consolidating requires more effort than a first step warrants.

PE-003.stem: Your agent achieves 55% first-contact resolution, well below the 80% target. Logs show it prioritizes simple cases while attempting to autonomously handle complex situations that require policy exceptions. How should escalation calibration be improved?

options.text: Add explicit escalation criteria to the system prompt with concise examples of when to escalate and when to resolve autonomously.
Have the agent state its confidence (1-10) and redirect to a human when it falls below a threshold.
Train a separate classifier on historical tickets that predicts which requests need escalation.
Apply sentiment analysis and escalate when frustration exceeds a threshold.

PE-003.rationale: The root cause is unclear decision boundaries. B fails because the LLM's self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated. C is overengineered. D solves a different problem.

PE-004.stem: You want to create a /review command that runs your team's review checklist and is available to all developers when they clone the repository. Where should the file be created?

options.text: In the project repository's .claude/commands/ directory.
In ~/.claude/commands/ in each developer's home directory.
In the CLAUDE.md file at the project root.
In a .claude/config.json file with a commands array.

PE-004.rationale: Project-scoped commands live in .claude/commands/, are version-controlled, and become automatically available. B is for personal commands. C is for project instructions, not command definitions. D describes a nonexistent mechanism.

PE-005.stem: You are assigned to restructure a monolithic application into microservices. It will involve changes across dozens of files and decisions about service boundaries and module dependencies. What approach should you adopt?

options.text: Plan mode to explore the code, understand dependencies, and design the approach before making changes.
Direct execution with incremental changes, letting implementation reveal the natural boundaries.
Direct execution with exhaustive upfront instructions detailing how to structure each service.
Start in direct execution and switch to plan mode only if unexpected complexity appears.

PE-005.rationale: Plan Mode exists for complex tasks with large-scale changes, multiple valid approaches, and architectural decisions. B risks costly rework. C presumes knowing the correct structure without exploration. D ignores that the complexity is already defined.

PE-006.stem: Test files are scattered throughout the codebase next to the code they test. You want all tests to follow the same conventions regardless of location. What is the simplest way?

options.text: Create rule files in .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter specifying glob patterns.
Consolidate all conventions in the root CLAUDE.md under per-area headings.
Create skills in .claude/skills/ per code type with the conventions in their SKILL.md.
Place a separate CLAUDE.md in each subdirectory with that area's conventions.

PE-006.rationale: Globs (e.g., **/*.test.tsx) apply conventions based on paths regardless of directory. B relies on inference. C requires manual invocation. D does not handle scattered files well.

PE-007.stem: On 'the impact of AI on creative industries,' each subagent completes successfully, but the report only covers visual arts. The coordinator broke the topic down into: digital art creation, graphic design, and photography. What is the most likely root cause?

options.text: The synthesis agent lacks instructions to identify coverage gaps.
The coordinator's task decomposition is too narrow and does not cover all relevant domains.
The web search agent's queries are not comprehensive enough.
The document analysis agent filters out non-visual sources using overly restrictive relevance criteria.

PE-007.rationale: The coordinator's logs reveal the cause: it decomposed 'creative industries' into visual-arts-only subtasks. The subagents correctly executed what they were assigned.

PE-008.stem: The web search subagent times out while investigating a complex topic. Which error-propagation approach enables intelligent recovery?

options.text: Return structured error context with failure type, attempted query, partial results, and alternative approaches.
Retry with exponential backoff inside the subagent and return a generic 'search unavailable' once retries are exhausted.
Catch the timeout and return an empty result set marked as successful.
Propagate the exception to a higher-level handler that terminates the entire research flow.

PE-008.rationale: Structured context gives the coordinator what it needs to decide on recovery. B hides valuable information. C suppresses the error and prevents any recovery. D terminates the flow unnecessarily.

PE-010.stem: The pipeline script runs claude "Analyze this pull request for security issues" but the job hangs indefinitely waiting for interactive input. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Add the -p flag.
Set the CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true environment variable.
Redirect stdin from /dev/null.
Add the --batch flag.

PE-010.rationale: -p (--print) is the documented way to run in non-interactive mode. B and D are nonexistent features. C is a Unix workaround that does not correctly address Claude Code's syntax.

PE-011.stem: Two workflows: (1) a pre-merge check that blocks and must complete before developers can merge, and (2) a nightly technical-debt report to be reviewed in the morning. Your manager proposes moving both to the Message Batches API for the 50% savings. How should you evaluate this?

options.text: Use batch processing only for the technical-debt report; keep real-time calls for the pre-merge check.
Switch both to batches with status polling to check completion.
Keep both real-time to avoid result-ordering issues.
Switch both to batches with a real-time fallback if they take too long.

PE-011.rationale: The Message Batches API takes up to 24h with no guaranteed SLA: unsuitable for blocking a merge, ideal for overnight work. B relies on completion that is 'often faster,' unacceptable for blocking workflows. C reflects a misunderstanding: results are correlated via custom_id.

PE-012.stem: A PR modifies 14 files. A single-pass review produces detailed comments for some files, superficial ones for others, misses obvious errors, and includes contradictory comments. How should the review be restructured?

options.text: Split into focused passes: analyze each file individually, then a separate integration pass that examines data flow across files.
Require developers to split large PRs into submissions of 3-4 files.
Switch to a model with a larger context window to give the 14 files adequate attention in a single pass.
Run three independent passes over the whole PR and flag only issues that appear in at least two.

PE-012.rationale: Splitting into specific phases addresses attention dilution. B shifts the burden onto the developer. C misunderstands that a larger context window does not fix attention quality. D would suppress detection of real errors that only appear intermittently.

PE-013.stem: Your loop checks whether Claude's response text contains the phrase 'I have completed' to decide whether to stop. What is the main problem with this termination method?

options.text: The agent will never terminate because process_refund always returns a success message that prevents the phrase from appearing.
Relying on natural-language signals is unreliable; you should inspect stop_reason and terminate only when it is 'end_turn'.
The loop should terminate as soon as any tool call fails, because continuing will corrupt the history.
Checking the text only works in synchronous mode; asynchronous contexts require a callback handler.

PE-013.rationale: stop_reason is the canonical method: iterate while it is 'tool_use', stop at 'end_turn'. Claude's phrasing varies across responses and prompt updates. D confuses asynchronous execution patterns with loop control logic.

PE-014.stem: A colleague proposes adding an iteration limit: if the loop has not finished after 15 tool calls, terminate with a generic 'research incomplete' response. What is the correct characterization of this design?

options.text: Iteration limits are the recommended primary stopping mechanism because they prevent excessive costs.
They are a reasonable safety limit for long tasks, but not the primary termination mechanism; stop_reason: 'end_turn' remains the authoritative signal.
It should be replaced by a time-based timeout, since token counting is more reliable.
Limits are unnecessary if the agent is instructed to request only the minimum tools needed.

PE-014.rationale: Treating the cap as the primary mechanism means the loop can interrupt legitimate multi-step research. D confuses prompt guidance with loop control: even a well-guided agent may need many calls.

PE-015.stem: A colleague suggests storing all tool results in a separate database and passing only a summary to the model on each iteration, instead of the full result. When would this most degrade agent performance?

options.text: When the results contain binary data such as images or attachments.
When the model needs to simultaneously analyze results from several tools to decide its next action, because summaries may omit necessary details.
When calls exceed 10 per session, because long histories slow down the API.
When tools return results in under 200 ms.

PE-015.rationale: The agentic loop depends on results being in the history so the model can reason about what was found before deciding. Summaries may omit field values, error codes, or conditional data. A is a valid concern but not the primary risk in text-based tasks.

PE-016.stem: Your coordinator routes every query through all four subagents regardless of complexity. For 'What year was the Anthropic API released?' the system takes 45 seconds. Which change addresses this most directly?

options.text: Replace the coordinator with a static routing table that maps keywords to subagent flows.
Have each subagent evaluate its own relevance and decide whether to opt in or out of the flow.
Design the coordinator to dynamically select which subagents to invoke based on query complexity and type.
Reduce from four to two subagents by merging web search and document analysis into a single retrieval agent.

PE-016.rationale: A replaces adaptive intelligence with a brittle keyword table. B distributes coordination logic across subagents, breaking the hub-and-spoke model and reducing observability. D reduces capability instead of improving routing.

PE-017.stem: The coordinator observes that the analysis subagent only processed three of the five specified sources. It needs the remaining two analyzed. What is the correct approach for re-delegating?

options.text: Invoke synthesis with the partial findings and instruct it to infer the likely content of the missing sources.
Re-invoke the analysis subagent with an explicit request specifying only the two missing sources, including the prior findings as context.
Send all five sources again to a new instance of the subagent.
Have the coordinator generate its own analysis of the two remaining sources.

PE-017.rationale: Evaluating results and reassigning specific tasks is the coordinator's function. A forces synthesis to fabricate content. C wastes resources by reprocessing. D ignores the subagent's specialization.

PE-019.stem: The web search subagent returns results without identifying which sources correspond to which claims, and the synthesis agent cannot produce reports with proper citations. What is the correct fix at the context-passing step?

options.text: Instruct the synthesis agent to perform its own web searches to locate the sources.
Use structured formats that separate claim content from metadata (URL, dates, page numbers) in the subagent's output, and include that structure when passing context.
Have the coordinator concatenate all outputs into a single block of text before sending it to synthesis.
Have the subagent return only the URLs and have the synthesis agent reread each source to reconstruct the findings.

PE-019.rationale: Separating content from metadata preserves source-claim associations during handoff. A introduces redundant work. C risks losing the associations through concatenation. D is extremely inefficient.

PE-020.stem: A coordinator needs to research three independent subtopics in parallel: market trends, competitive analysis, and regulatory environment. How should it spawn subagents to maximize throughput?

options.text: Sequentially: start the first, wait for its result, then the second, to avoid context conflicts.
Issue all three Task tool calls in a single coordinator response, enabling parallel execution.
Route all three subtopics through a single subagent sequentially, sharing context between them.
Use a single subagent with three prompts in sequence, passing previous results as context.

PE-020.rationale: The Agent SDK supports parallel execution by issuing multiple Task calls in a single response. A introduces unnecessary serial latency. C assumes a dependency the question does not establish. D eliminates parallelism.

PE-021.stem: The account-closure flow requires: (1) verifying identity with get_customer, (2) checking subscriptions with check_subscriptions, (3) closing with close_account. Logs show the agent occasionally calls close_account before verifying identity. A colleague suggests adding to the system prompt: 'Always verify identity before closing accounts.' What is the most effective approach?

options.text: The system prompt instruction is sufficient because it explicitly describes the required order.
Add few-shot examples with the correct sequence alongside the instruction.
Implement a programmatic prerequisite that blocks close_account until get_customer has returned a verified ID.
Add a routing classifier that preselects the appropriate tools before the agent begins.

PE-021.rationale: When ordering has severe consequences (unauthorized closures), programmatic enforcement provides deterministic guarantees. A relies on probabilistic compliance, which logs already show is insufficient. B improves odds without guaranteeing. D addresses selection, not ordering.

PE-022.stem: A customer raises three issues in a single message: a billing dispute, a lost order, and an email update. The agent processes them sequentially, taking 3-4 minutes per request. Which change most improves efficiency without compromising accuracy?

options.text: Handle only the highest-priority issue per turn and ask for separate tickets for the rest.
Break the three concerns into distinct research items and process them in parallel using the customer's shared context, then compile a unified response.
Process them sequentially but cache the intermediate results.
Delegate all three to a single subagent specialized in 'multiple issues'.

PE-022.rationale: Independent concerns processed in parallel drastically reduce latency by using the customer context already retrieved. A creates a poor experience. C improves caching but does not eliminate the serial bottleneck. D creates an undifferentiated subagent that does not reflect the specialization pattern.

PE-023.stem: Three MCP tools return heterogeneous formats: Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 dates, and numeric status codes (1=active, 2=paused, 3=canceled). The agent misinterprets these formats. What is the most appropriate architectural solution?

options.text: Update each backend system to return a uniform format before the agent calls them.
Add conversion instructions to the system prompt explaining how to interpret each convention.
Implement PostToolUse hooks that intercept results from each source and normalize timestamps, dates, and codes before the model processes them.
Add post-processing after the agent's final response to reformat dates and statuses.

PE-023.rationale: PostToolUse is the mechanism for intercepting and transforming results before the model processes them. A requires backend changes that may be infeasible and introduces coupling. B relies on probabilistic compliance. D normalizes after the model has already reasoned over inconsistent data.

PE-024.stem: Policy: refunds over $500 require manager approval. The system prompt states this, but logs show noncompliance in ~3% of cases. What is the most effective way to guarantee compliance?

options.text: Strengthen the message: 'It is strictly prohibited to process refunds over $500 without explicit approval under any circumstances.'
Add 10 few-shot examples showing how to request approval for high-value refunds.
Implement a hook that intercepts outgoing calls to process_refund, checks the amount, and blocks or redirects to the approval flow when it exceeds $500.
Implement a post-hoc validation that reverses any refund that exceeded the threshold.

PE-024.rationale: Business rules requiring guaranteed compliance must be enforced programmatically. A and B improve probability without guaranteeing zero violations. D runs after the fact: the violation has already occurred.

PE-025.stem: A PostToolUse hook transforms Bash output: it adds a formatted summary but also retains the full raw output. Sessions exploring large codebases hit context limits sooner than expected. Which change most reduces unnecessary consumption?

options.text: Disable the hook entirely and let the model process the raw Bash output unformatted.
Modify the hook to return only the formatted summary, trimming the raw output instead of keeping it alongside the summary.
Increase max_tokens to accommodate the additional context from both outputs.
Switch from PostToolUse hooks to preprocessing Bash commands to produce shorter output.

PE-025.rationale: PostToolUse hooks can trim verbose output. Keeping both raw and summarized doubles consumption per call. A eliminates the benefits of normalization. C increases output capacity without addressing input context. D would require significant, possibly infeasible changes.

PE-026.stem: Code review must cover three aspects per PR: security vulnerabilities, style compliance, and performance implications. Each aspect has clear, documented criteria. What is the most appropriate decomposition strategy?

options.text: Dynamic adaptive decomposition: the agent scans the entire PR and generates a review plan based on its findings.
Prompt chaining with sequential focused passes: one per aspect, each with specific criteria.
A single comprehensive pass that examines all three aspects simultaneously to capture cross-cutting concerns.
Spawn three fully independent agents with no shared context and merge their results at the end.

PE-026.rationale: With predictable, well-defined aspects, chaining with focused passes is the pattern. A uses dynamic decomposition for a flow with known structure. C suffers the attention dilution that chaining resolves. D loses integration context across files.

PE-027.stem: The system must determine the root cause of a bug introduced at some point during the last two weeks, across an unknown set of files and services. The scope cannot be known in advance. Which decomposition method is most appropriate?

options.text: Prompt chaining: design a fixed sequence of steps (review logs, read configurations, trace calls) that the agent executes in order.
Dynamic adaptive decomposition: first map the affected services and the timeline, then generate and prioritize subtasks based on what is discovered at each step.
Split the work between two agents: one reads logs, the other reads source code, each reporting independently to a human.
Run an exhaustive search of all files modified in the past two weeks and produce a ranked list for manual review.

PE-027.rationale: Open-ended investigations require the agent to build its plan from intermediate findings. A static chain does not adapt to unexpected dependencies. C removes the coordinating intelligence. D is a single-pass heuristic that does not apply the model's reasoning.

PE-028.stem: After several hours investigating a legacy authentication service, you need to pause the work. Three main files in the module will be modified overnight by another team. What is the most reliable method for resuming the next day?

options.text: Resume with --resume <session-name> and notify the agent about the specific files that were modified, so it can re-analyze them in light of its prior understanding.
Start a new session, because stale results make resuming never reliable.
Resume without notifying about the changes; the agent will automatically detect the modifications when it reads those files.
Use fork_session to create a branch before stepping away and resume from the fork.

PE-028.rationale: B is overly conservative: starting from scratch is appropriate when results are stale overall, not when a few known files changed. C is incorrect: the agent does not automatically detect changes upon resuming. D misuses fork_session, which is meant for divergent approaches from a shared baseline.

PE-030.stem: lookup_order frequently returns errors: the agent enters free text like 'last Tuesday's order' instead of the required ISO-8601 format. The description reads: 'Retrieves order details from a date or an identifier,' with no examples or constraints. Which change most directly reduces these errors?

options.text: Add format constraints, accepted values, and input examples to the tool description.
Add to the system prompt: 'Always use ISO-8601 format when calling lookup_order.'
Add schema validation that rejects malformed inputs and returns an error to the agent.
Split into lookup_order_by_id and lookup_order_by_date to reduce ambiguity.

PE-030.rationale: The description is the primary mechanism for understanding how to call a tool. B adds overhead and is more fragile than a specific description. C validates but does not prevent the model from submitting bad inputs, creating error loops. D addresses disambiguation, not format guidance.

PE-031.stem: Three tools with similar names and descriptions: get_account_info ('Get information about the account'), fetch_account_details ('Look up account details'), and retrieve_customer_record ('Retrieve customer information'). They access different backends. The agent routes incorrectly. What resolves the misrouting?

options.text: Add a list to the system prompt of the three tools specifying when to use each.
Rename them to reflect their distinct data sources and rewrite the descriptions explaining what each returns, which backend it queries, and what use case it serves.
Consolidate the three into a single tool with a source parameter that specifies the backend.
Keep them and randomize which one the agent calls, combining the responses in post-processing.

PE-031.rationale: Overlapping names and descriptions cause misrouting. A can reduce errors but does not fix the root cause: the descriptions remain indistinguishable. C merges three specialized tools into one generic tool and shifts routing to the model in a less structured way. D is not a viable architecture.

PE-032.stem: process_refund returns the same response for every failure: {"status": "error", "message": "Operation failed"}. This is triggered by network timeouts, invalid amounts, fraud-detection blocks, and expired order IDs. Which design most improves the agent's recovery?

options.text: Return different HTTP status codes per failure type and have the agent interpret them.
Return structured metadata with an errorCategory (transient/validation/permission/business), a boolean isRetryable, and a reason-specific human-readable explanation.
Return a detailed log with the full stack trace and system state.
Return a numeric error code and have the system map each code to a recovery action.

PE-032.rationale: Structured metadata allows the agent to choose the correct path: retry a transient error, request corrected input on validation, or explain a policy block. A depends on HTTP semantics that don't map to every category. C consumes context without improving the decision. D encodes the logic in the prompt rather than in the error's structure.

PE-033.stem: search_web returns {"results": [], "status": "success"} and the subagent reports 'search successful, no relevant results.' You later discover the API was down and was returning empty results for every query. Which change would prevent this confusion?

options.text: Always return a non-empty array, including fallback content whenever the actual search returns nothing.
Distinguish access failures (could not be reached, or returned an error) from valid empty results (the search succeeded with no matches), using the isError flag for the former.
Add a confidence field so the agent can infer whether the empty result is real or a failure.
Implement automatic retries inside the MCP tool itself so the agent never sees an empty result except after they are exhausted.

PE-033.rationale: These are fundamentally different conditions that call for different responses. A masks failures by fabricating content. C introduces ambiguity: a confidence score over a genuinely empty result makes no sense. D handles retries locally but does not resolve the inability to distinguish the cases.

PE-034.stem: check_fraud_risk returns {"isError": true, "message": "Refund blocked"} when the fraud system flags a refund. The agent interprets this as transient and retries three times, generating three compliance alerts. What is missing from the response design?

options.text: A retry_after timestamp so the agent knows when to retry.
isRetryable: false plus a client-appropriate explanation that distinguishes this business-rule block from a transient error.
Suppress the isError flag on fraud blocks and return success with a blocked: true field.
Include the risk score so the agent can decide whether it is high enough to justify the block.

PE-034.rationale: A business-rule block is unrecoverable; isRetryable: false prevents redundant attempts that trigger alerts. A implies the block is temporary. C hides the error's nature. D gives the agent data it may not be authorized to act on.

PE-035.stem: You gave the synthesis agent access to all 18 tools in the system (web search, file reading, database queries, email, calendar), arguing that more tools provide more flexibility. Which problem is most likely?

options.text: The agent will refuse to call any tool, overwhelmed by the options.
Having tools outside its specialization increases the likelihood of misuse, such as launching new web searches instead of synthesizing the results already provided.
18 tools will exceed the context window limit for schemas, causing API errors.
The additional tools will slow the agent down because it must read every description before producing output.

PE-035.rationale: A overstates the effect: the agent will still call tools, but may call the wrong ones. C is not a realistic failure mode for 18 typical schemas. D mischaracterizes how descriptions affect latency.

PE-036.stem: Every response from the draft_response agent must include a structured JSON summary. You want to guarantee it calls generate_summary on every invocation, not optionally. Which tool_choice configuration achieves this?

options.text: tool_choice: "auto" so the model decides when the summary is needed.
tool_choice: "any" so it must call at least one tool, though it may pick a different one.
tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "generate_summary"} to force that specific tool.
Remove all other tools so generate_summary is the only option.

PE-036.rationale: Forced selection by name guarantees that tool on every invocation. 'auto' allows returning text without calling anything. 'any' guarantees a call but not which one. D achieves the outcome indirectly but removes legitimate tools the agent needs for other tasks.

PE-037.stem: You are setting up a shared GitHub MCP server for all engineers. It requires an API token. You want everyone to have it upon cloning the repository with no manual configuration, and you want to avoid committing the token to version control. Which configuration is correct?

options.text: Add the server to each machine's ~/.claude.json with its personal token hardcoded.
Add the server to the project-scoped .mcp.json with the token via environment variable expansion (for example, ${GITHUB_TOKEN}), and commit .mcp.json to the repository.
Add the configuration to the root CLAUDE.md in an [mcp_servers] section.
Create a setup script that each developer runs once to add it to their own ~/.claude.json.

PE-037.rationale: The correct pattern is a project-scoped .mcp.json with variable expansion: it is committed so everyone gets it, and tokens are injected at runtime. A and D require manual per-person configuration. C describes a mechanism that does not exist in CLAUDE.md.

PE-038.stem: An agent makes multiple exploratory calls to discover which data sources are available on your MCP server before it can respond. This increases latency and consumes context. Which MCP feature addresses this most directly?

options.text: Add a list_tools meta-tool that returns all available names and descriptions.
Expose the content catalogs as MCP Resources, letting the agent see what data is available upon connecting instead of through exploratory calls.
Reduce the number of tools by merging similar ones to minimize the discovery surface.
Add a caching layer that stores the results of prior exploratory calls and reuses them across sessions.

PE-038.rationale: MCP Resources expose catalogs so the agent knows what's available without exploratory calls. A would still require a call to discover them. C reduces functionality to work around a structural problem. D addresses the symptom, and caching across sessions can return stale data.

PE-039.stem: You need to find every TypeScript file in a project with thousands of files that imports from a deprecated module called legacy-auth. Which tool combination is most appropriate?

options.text: Bash with find . -name "*.ts" and then Bash again with grep on each file found.
Glob to find all .ts files, then Read to open each file and check the import.
Grep to search for the import pattern across all TypeScript files in the codebase.
Read on the root directory to get a file listing, then recursive Read on each subdirectory.

PE-039.rationale: Grep is the tool for searching content across the codebase. A uses shell commands that should be replaced by dedicated tools. B enumerates and then reads every file, far less efficient. D uses Read to traverse directories, an unsupported use.

PE-040.stem: When using Edit, the tool returns: 'Non-unique match: 3 occurrences of the target text were found.' What is the correct alternative method?

options.text: Use Bash to run a sed command that replaces all occurrences simultaneously.
Use Read to load the full file, identify the exact surrounding context needed to make the edit unique, and retry Edit with a larger old_string.
Use Write to overwrite the entire file with a corrected version based on the content loaded by Read.
Use Grep to locate the line number of each occurrence and then use Edit with a line-number parameter.

PE-040.rationale: The first step when text is not unique is to read the file and construct a unique old_string. C (Read + Write) is a valid alternative, but only when Edit cannot find a unique anchor even with additional context. A would replace every occurrence. D describes a parameter Edit does not support.

PE-041.stem: A senior engineer adds coding standards and security guidelines to their ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. A new team member clones the repository and reports that Claude Code is not following the team's documented standards. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The new member's version of Claude Code is outdated and does not support shared configuration files.
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is user-scoped and is not under version control, so teammates do not receive it when cloning.
CLAUDE.md files must be placed inside the .claude/ subdirectory to be recognized; the root-level one is ignored.
The hierarchy requires the project file to explicitly import from the user file with @import.

PE-041.rationale: User-scoped configuration applies only to the individual developer and never enters version control. To share it, those instructions belong in the project's CLAUDE.md or .claude/CLAUDE.md. A and D describe mechanisms that do not exist. C is incorrect: a root-level CLAUDE.md is a valid project location.

PE-042.stem: Your monorepo has a root CLAUDE.md of more than 400 lines covering Python, TypeScript, infrastructure, and testing conventions. Claude sometimes applies the wrong conventions to the wrong files. What is the best reorganization?
